skill.name: Work out a word's meaning from the words around it
skill.why: When you meet a tricky word, the words around it often explain it.
skill.how: Read the sentence and the next one. Find the clues, guess, then test your guess.

beats.say: Stuck on a word? Don't panic. Look at its neighbours.
beats.show: After footy, Jai was **ravenous**. He ate four pies.

beats.say: Ask: what do the other words tell me?
beats.show: Jai was ravenous. **He ate four pies.**

beats.say: Four pies? He must be really, really hungry.
Now test it. Put your guess where the word was.
beats.show: After footy, Jai was **really hungry**. He ate four pies.

beats.say: Still makes sense? Then you've cracked it.

Nothing in the sentence is about speed. Zed fell asleep, so it's about being tired.

creature.name: Tintacle
creature.blurb: A giant cuttlefish that changes colour to match whatever is around it. It works out what a word means the same way: from its neighbours.

encounters.frame: Mo's cooking diary has a word the Tintacle doesn't know.
encounters.text: Day 12. Today I made toast for the crew. I wanted it golden and crunchy. Then Tully started telling me about the Reef Rays. I forgot all about the toast. Smoke filled the galley and the alarm went off. The toast was scorched. It was black on both sides and as hard as a roof tile. Gus ate his anyway. He said it tasted like a campfire. Wren fed hers to a seagull. The seagull spat it out.
encounters.success: Burnt black. The smoke, the alarm and the black sides all tell you the toast burnt.

options.reason: Nothing says the toast was cut. The smoke and the black sides tell you it burnt.

encounters.frame: Gus left his lab report open. The Tintacle has turned a worried green.
encounters.text: Experiment 47: The Sock Jar. I sealed one of Mo's footy socks in a jar for three weeks. On day one, it smelled a bit like cheese. By day ten, a grey fuzz had grown over the heel. On day twenty-one, I opened the lid. The smell was so pungent that it made my eyes water from across the room. Wren ran outside gasping for air. The Tintacle turned a sickly green and hid under the bench. Even with every window open, the lab stank for two whole days. Result: never open the jar again. Mo has asked for his sock back. The answer is no.
encounters.success: Strong and sharp. The smell made eyes water from across the room and the lab stank for days.

options.reason: A faint smell wouldn't make your eyes water from across the room.
Wren ran out gasping and the lab stank, so it wasn't a nice smell.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing tips for his speedrun stream.
encounters.text: Level 9 of Lava Tower is the hardest part of my speedrun. The fireballs are relentless. They never stop, not even for a second. As soon as you dodge one, three more come flying at you. Most players try to wait for a gap, but there is no gap. I learned to keep running and jump every two beats of the music. My best time is four minutes and twelve seconds. My thumbs were sore for a whole day afterwards. Next week I'm going to try it with my eyes shut. Mo says that is a terrible idea, and that I'll just fall in the lava a lot.

options.reason: Size isn't the clue. The fireballs never stop and there's no gap.

encounters.frame: Tully is reading her match report out loud. Twice.
encounters.text: Herons Win the Netball Grand Final! With five seconds left, the scores were level. Then Kira Bell caught a pass right under the ring. She leapt and shot, and the ball dropped through without touching the sides. The buzzer went, and the Herons had won by one goal! The crowd was jubilant. Fans hugged total strangers. Some cried happy tears, and one man threw his hat so high that it landed on the scoreboard. Down on the court, the Herons players hugged each other in a big, sweaty pile. encounters.frame: Wren's diary, written the morning after a bat count.
encounters.text: Last night I went to count the bats in the old mine. Everything about it was eerie. The wind made a low moaning sound through the tunnels. Water dripped somewhere in the dark, but I couldn't see where. My torch flickered. The hairs on my arms stood up, and I kept feeling that someone was standing right behind me. When I turned around, nobody was there. I counted the bats as fast as I could. Then I ran all the way back to the boat without looking behind me. This morning Gus asked if I wanted to go back tonight for a second count. I said no thanks.

options.reason: Her torch flickered in the dark and she ran away. Nothing was cheerful.

encounters.frame: Indi's sketchbook has a before-and-after page about her new mural.
encounters.text: Before: The wall behind the island shop used to be the dullest thing I had ever seen. It was the grey of old porridge, and the paint was peeling off in sad little curls. Nobody ever stopped to look at it. After: Last week the shop owner let me paint a mural. I used hot pink for the coral, electric blue for the waves and a yellow so bright it almost hummed. I added orange fish with lime-green stripes. Now the wall is so vibrant that people walking past stop in their tracks. A kid on a scooter crashed into a bin because he was staring at it. (He was fine.) The shop owner says her sales have doubled. The Tintacle sat in front of it for an hour, flashing every colour it could, trying to keep up. Tully says it's the brightest thing on the island, and that includes her Reef Rays scarf.

encounters.frame: Wren's rescue log. The Tintacle is still flashing duck-yellow.
encounters.text: Rescue Log, Thursday. At 4 pm we got a call about a mother duck in the island car park. Her six ducklings had tumbled through a drain grate, and she couldn't reach them. When we arrived, she was frantic. She was racing back and forth across the grate, quacking at the top of her voice and flapping so hard that feathers flew everywhere. She didn't even notice the cars beeping at her. Her ducklings were peeping from the dark water below, and that only made her worse. Gus lifted the grate with a crowbar, and I lay on my stomach and scooped the ducklings out one by one with a fishing net. They were wet and cheeping, but nobody was hurt. The moment the last one was out, the mother duck went completely quiet. She tucked them under her wings and sat down as if nothing had happened. Mo says she looked a bit smug.
encounters.success: Wild with worry. Her ducklings were trapped, so she raced about, quacked and flapped until they were safe.

options.reason: Racing back and forth and flapping isn't patient. She only went calm at the end.
She was like this before the crew did anything. Her trapped ducklings were the cause.
She wasn't searching for food. She was racing over the grate where her ducklings were trapped.

encounters.frame: A crackly message reaches the boat from a very lonely rover.
encounters.text: Day 400 on Planet Kreeb. This is Rover Pip, reporting to Earth. In every direction there is nothing but red dust and grey rock. There are no trees, no rivers and no animals. I have not seen a single living thing since I landed. My cameras still work perfectly, but there is nothing to film. I have counted every rock within a kilometre. There are 9,412, and none of them can talk. The wind blows all day, but there is nobody to hear it except me. At night the only light comes from two tiny moons, and it drops to ninety degrees below zero. This is the most desolate place I have ever explored. Yesterday I found a rock shaped like a sandwich and got very excited. It was just a rock. Sometimes I play my landing song just to hear a sound that isn't wind. Please send a friend. Even a small one. Even a toaster.
encounters.success: Empty and lonely. There's nothing alive, nobody to hear the wind, and Pip begs for a friend.

options.reason: Pip hasn't seen a single living thing since landing.
There's only red dust, grey rock and the light of two tiny moons.
It drops to ninety degrees below zero at night, so it isn't hot.

encounters.frame: Mo wrote about the island busking contest for the crew newsletter.
encounters.text: The Hollowgum Busking Contest had been noisy all day. Kids shouted, a dog barked at a drummer, and somebody's ukulele was badly out of tune. A juggler dropped three of his fish, and a seagull stole one. Then an old woman sat down on an upturned bucket and began to play a silver flute. Her music was soft and slow, like water running over stones. Within seconds, the whole crowd was mesmerised. Nobody talked. Nobody checked their phone. A boy holding an ice cream didn't notice it melting down his arm. Even the barking dog lay down and stared at her with its head on one side. When the last note faded, there was a long silence before anyone remembered to clap. She won first prize, a bucket of prawns, and played one more tune for free. This time the dog howled along. The juggler has asked her for flute lessons.
encounters.success: So fascinated they couldn't look away. Nobody talked, the boy forgot his ice cream and even the dog stared.

options.text: so fascinated they couldn't look away

options.reason: Bored people chat and check their phones. Here nobody did, and the boy forgot his ice cream.
The noisy part came before the flute. Once she played, everyone went still to listen.
Nothing in the text is about rules. Everyone was staring at the flute player.

encounters.frame: Zed's diary, written by torchlight in the back of the boat.
encounters.text: Night three on Hollowgum Island. We had planned to camp at the old quarry, but from the moment we arrived, everything felt ominous. A thick fog rolled in off the water and swallowed the path behind us. The birds, which had been squawking all afternoon, suddenly went completely silent, as if someone had switched them off. Even the frogs had stopped croaking. My torch started to flicker. Far below in the quarry, something was clanking slowly, like a chain being dragged over rock. Gus said it was probably old machinery moving in the wind, but there wasn't any wind. Then the Tintacle, which never stops flashing colours, turned a flat, dull black and squeezed itself into the bottom of my backpack. Wren whispered that animals often know when something bad is about to happen. That was when we found the sign. Someone had scratched out the words 'Quarry Closed' and written underneath, in fresh red paint, 'Turn back while you can.' We didn't argue. We packed up the tents in about four minutes, which Tully says is a crew record, and we didn't stop running until we could see the lights of the boat. None of us said a word on the way back. Mo claims he wasn't scared, but he slept with the torch on.
encounters.success: Threatening, as if something bad is coming. Silent birds, clanking and a warning sign all hint at danger ahead.

options.text: threatening, as if something bad is coming

options.reason: Fog and silence might sound calm, but the crew ran for the boat. The clues point to danger.
Clanking chains and a red warning sign aren't boring. The clues point to danger.
Nobody is missing or left behind. The silent birds and warning sign point to danger, not sadness.

encounters.frame: Tully's report on the under-12 soccer final. She's still shouting about it.
encounters.text: It all came down to the final penalty. If Harbour Heights scored, they would win the cup, but if our goalkeeper, Sami, saved it, the match would go to sudden death. Every single person in the stands was on their feet, chewing their nails or hiding their eyes behind their hands. Sami, on the other hand, looked completely nonchalant. While the striker placed the ball on the spot, Sami leaned against the goalpost, yawned and retied a bootlace as if he were waiting for a bus. He even waved to his nan in the crowd. His nan, who was the only calm person in the stands apart from Sami, waved back. Our coach was turning purple on the sideline, shouting at him to concentrate. The striker took a long run-up and blasted the ball towards the top corner. Sami simply stepped to his left and caught it against his chest. The crowd went wild, and the Harbour Heights striker sank to the grass with her hands over her face. Sami just shrugged, rolled the ball to the referee and wandered back to his line. Afterwards, a reporter asked him how he had stayed so relaxed. Sami said, 'It's only a game. Is there any orange cake left?'
encounters.success: Calm and not bothered at all. 'On the other hand' sets Sami's yawning and waving against the crowd's nerves.

options.text: calm and not bothered at all

options.reason: That was the crowd, chewing their nails. Sami yawned and retied his bootlace.
The coach was the one turning purple. Sami was busy waving to his nan.
Sami knew exactly what to do. He stepped left and caught the ball with no fuss.

encounters.frame: Gus's lab notebook. The cover says 'Warning: contains maggots'.
encounters.text: Experiment 82: Can black soldier fly larvae eat a whole watermelon in a day? Black soldier fly larvae are fat, pale grubs that farmers sometimes use to get rid of food scraps, because they will eat almost anything. At 9 am, I placed half a watermelon in a tub containing roughly two thousand larvae. Within ten minutes, the surface of the fruit was crawling and wriggling, and I could hear a faint crunching sound, like someone eating cereal in the next room. By lunchtime, the red flesh had become a soggy pink crater. By 5 pm, nothing was left but a thin, chewed rind, and the larvae were still searching for more. When I lowered a banana skin into the tub, it vanished under a heaving pile of grubs in under a minute. These are the most voracious eaters I have ever studied. Mo asked whether they could clean up the galley after one of his cooking disasters. I said yes, as long as he didn't mind them eating the tablecloth too. Wren made me promise to keep the lid on the tub at night, just in case. Conclusion: yes, they can finish a watermelon in a day, with room to spare. Next experiment: a whole pumpkin.
encounters.success: Wanting to eat huge amounts. They ate half a watermelon in a day and still searched for more.

options.reason: Within ten minutes the fruit was crawling, and it was gone by 5 pm. That's fast, not slow.
Gus says they will eat almost anything, maybe even a tablecloth. That isn't fussy.
Nothing says they harm people. The clues are all about how much and how fast they eat.

encounters.frame: Maxx Vantablack is live-streaming again. The crew is watching on Zed's tablet.
encounters.text: 'Hey, Vantafam! Maxx here, coming to you live from Hollowgum Island, where I have just personally rescued forty-seven rare Creatures with my bare hands!' Maxx held up an empty cage and grinned at the camera. 'They were so grateful that they all flew off to freedom, which is why you can't see any of them right now. Smash that like button!' Behind him, something in the bushes squeaked, and a small furry paw poked out of a sack before Maxx quickly nudged the sack out of shot with his foot. On the boat, the crew were dubious. Gus raised one eyebrow so high it nearly left his face. Tully pointed out that catching forty-seven Creatures would take about a week, and Maxx had only arrived on the island that morning. Wren noticed that the cage still had a price sticker on it. Indi paused the stream and zoomed in on Maxx's boots, which were spotless, even though he claimed to have spent hours wading through mud. Mo pointed out that Maxx's hands, which had supposedly caught forty-seven Creatures, didn't have a single scratch. 'So,' said Mo slowly, 'we don't believe him, right?' Nobody even bothered to answer. Zed was already scrolling through the comments, looking for anyone else who had spotted the sticker.
encounters.success: Doubtful that it was true. Each crew member spots a clue that Maxx is lying, and nobody believes him.

options.reason: Impressed people would cheer. The crew checked the sticker, the boots and the timing instead.
Nobody wishes they were Maxx. They're hunting for proof that he's lying.
Raising an eyebrow and zooming in on his boots isn't fear. They're checking whether he's telling the truth.
